learn.hook: Can one child clean a whole muddy path? Maybe not. But what about four children?
points: The lesson 'Together We Can' is about friends who do a big job by working as a team.
Teamwork means people work together to reach one goal.
When everyone does a small part, a big job becomes easy.
To answer a question about a story, find the line that gives the answer.
The title of a story often tells us its main idea.

example.q: Read: The rain had washed mud all over the school path in Mysuru. "It is too much for me," sighed Meera. Then Arjun brought a broom, Salma brought a bucket and Tenzin brought a spade. Everyone took one small job. By lunch, the path was clean. "Alone we are small," smiled their teacher, "but together we can!" Question: How did the children clean the path so quickly?
steps: Look for the line about the work: 'Everyone took one small job.'
So each child did one part of the work.
Many hands together finished the big job fast.
example.answer: They shared the work. Each child did one small job.

learn.reallife: Cleaning the classroom, making a rangoli for a school festival or playing kabaddi: all of these need teamwork.

games.title: Story order
games.prompt: Put the story in the right order
items: Rain washed mud onto the path
Meera sighed that the job was too big
Arjun, Salma and Tenzin brought tools
The path was clean by lunch

games.title: Teamwork: true or false?
items: In a team, everyone can do a part of the job.
When each person does a part, the work gets done faster.
Teamwork means one person does all the work.
Teamwork means many people work together.
Sharing tools is one way to cooperate.
When we share, everyone can help with the job.
Good team members listen to each other.
Listening helps the team agree on a plan.
Laughing at a teammate's mistake helps the team.
Laughing at someone hurts them. Kind words help the team.

quiz.q: Story line: "Arjun brought a broom, Salma brought a bucket and Tenzin brought a spade." What did Salma bring?
quiz.explain: The line says 'Salma brought a bucket'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which child brought which tool

quiz.q: Story line: "The rain had washed mud all over the school path." What made the path dirty?
quiz.explain: The rain washed mud onto the path.
quiz.mistake: Guesses instead of reading the line

quiz.q: Meera sighed, "It is too much for me." How did Meera feel at first?
options: Worried that the job was too big
quiz.explain: 'It is too much for me' and a sigh show she felt the job was too big for one person.
quiz.mistake: Does not use the word 'sighed' and the words she said as clues

quiz.q: Story line: "By lunch, the path was clean." When was the path clean?
quiz.explain: The story says the path was clean by lunch.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the time word in the line

quiz.q: The teacher says, "Alone we are small, but together we can!" What does she mean?
options: Small children cannot do any work
It is better to always work alone
Only teachers can do big jobs
We can do big jobs when we work together
quiz.explain: The teacher means that a group working together can do what one person cannot.
quiz.mistake: Takes the word 'small' to mean body size

quiz.q: In "Everyone took one small job," which word tells us that all the children helped?
quiz.explain: 'Everyone' means all the people, so all the children helped.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word without thinking about its meaning

quiz.q: Which is the best title for the story about the muddy school path?
quiz.explain: The story is about friends cleaning the path together, so this title tells the main idea.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a title about one small detail instead of the main idea

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of teamwork?
options: Ravi eats his tiffin by himself
Four friends carry a heavy bench together
quiz.explain: Carrying a bench together means people are working as a team.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that teamwork needs people working together

teach.ask: Gappu wants to build a big nest but it is too hard alone. What is teamwork, and how can it help Gappu?
teach.praise: Yes! When friends work together and each does a part, a big job becomes easy. Gappu will call his friends!
teach.nudge: What happens to a big job when everyone does one part of it?

learn.hook: 'Team' + 'work' makes 'teamwork'. Two small words can join to make a new one!
points: To cooperate means to work together and help each other.
Synonyms are words with the same or nearly the same meaning: help and assist.
Antonyms are words with opposite meanings: together and alone, strong and weak.
A compound word is made of two smaller words: team + work = teamwork, class + mate = classmate.

example.q: Think it through: what is the opposite of 'together' in this sentence? 'We cleaned the room together.'
steps: 'Together' means with other people.
The opposite would be with no one else.
The word for that is 'alone': 'I cleaned the room alone.'
example.answer: alone

learn.reallife: When your class plays tug of war, you cooperate with your classmates and pull together.

quiz.q: What does 'cooperate' mean?
quiz.explain: To cooperate is to work together and help each other.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'cooperate' with a word that sounds similar

quiz.q: Which word means the same as 'help'?
quiz.explain: 'Assist' is a synonym of 'help'.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what a synonym is

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'together'?
quiz.explain: 'Together' means with others; 'alone' means with no one.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word with the same meaning instead of the opposite

quiz.q: Which two words join to make 'teamwork'?
quiz.explain: teamwork = team + work.
quiz.mistake: Splits the compound word in the wrong place

quiz.q: Which of these is a compound word?
quiz.explain: classmate = class + mate, two smaller words joined together.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any long word is a compound word

quiz.q: Choose the right word: "Riya and Kabir ___ their crayons, so both can colour."
quiz.explain: When they share, both children can use the crayons.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the second part of the sentence

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'strong'?
quiz.explain: 'Weak' is the opposite of 'strong'. The other words mean almost the same as strong.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up synonyms and antonyms

quiz.q: "A big job becomes easy when many people help." Which word is the opposite of 'easy'?
quiz.explain: 'Difficult' means hard, the opposite of easy.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a word that means the same as easy

teach.ask: Gappu heard the word 'cooperate'. What does it mean? Can you tell Gappu a word that is opposite to 'together'?
teach.praise: Super! To cooperate is to work together, and the opposite of together is alone. Gappu learnt two words!
teach.nudge: What does 'cooperate' mean? And what is the opposite of 'together'?

topics.title: Naming words: common, proper and collective nouns

learn.hook: Meera, Mysuru, broom and team are all naming words. What kind of naming word is each?
points: A noun is a naming word. It names a person, place, animal or thing.
A common noun is a general name: girl, city, river, broom.
A proper noun is the special name of one person, place or thing: Meera, Mysuru, Ganga. It begins with a capital letter.
A collective noun names a group: a team of players, a flock of birds, a herd of elephants.
More groups: a swarm of bees, a bunch of grapes, a pack of wolves.

example.q: Think it through: find the nouns in 'A team of girls from Pune won a cup.'
steps: 'team' names a group, so it is a collective noun.
'girls' and 'cup' are general names, so they are common nouns.
'Pune' is the name of one particular city, so it is a proper noun.
example.answer: team (collective), girls and cup (common), Pune (proper)

learn.reallife: Your school name, your city and your best friend's name are proper nouns. Your school's cricket team is a collective noun!

quiz.q: Which of these is a proper noun?
quiz.explain: Chennai is the name of one particular city, so it is a proper noun.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any place word is a proper noun

quiz.q: Fill in: "A ___ of bees buzzed near the flowers."
quiz.explain: A group of bees is called a swarm.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up collective nouns for different animals

quiz.q: Which word is a collective noun?
quiz.explain: 'Team' names a group of players, so it is a collective noun.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that a collective noun names a group

quiz.q: In "Kabir lives in Shimla," which words are proper nouns?
quiz.explain: Kabir is a person's name and Shimla is a place's name. Both are proper nouns.
quiz.mistake: Picks words that are not naming words

quiz.q: Fill in: "A ___ of elephants crossed the river."
quiz.explain: A group of elephants is a herd.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'flock', which is for birds

quiz.q: In "my cousin lives in agra.", which word is a proper noun that needs a capital letter?
quiz.explain: Agra is the name of a particular city, so it is a proper noun and needs a capital A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a common noun like 'cousin' needs a capital letter

quiz.q: Which of these is a common noun?
quiz.explain: 'Mango' is a general name for a fruit. The others are special names.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up common and proper nouns

quiz.q: In "a team of players", what does the word 'team' name?
quiz.explain: 'Team' is a collective noun. It names a group.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a collective noun names one thing

teach.ask: Gappu is confused. Meera, girl and team are all nouns, but how are they different?
teach.praise: Brilliant! Meera is a proper noun, girl is a common noun and team is a collective noun for a group. Gappu loves nouns now!
teach.nudge: Which kind of noun names a group? And which one starts with a capital letter?

learn.hook: Close your eyes. Tinkle! Ding-dong! Jingle! Can you hear the bells just from the words?
points: 'The Tinkling Bells' is a poem full of the sounds that bells make.
Sound words are words that sound like the noise they name: tinkle, buzz, hiss, splash.
Animals have sound words too: a cow moos, a duck quacks, a bee buzzes, an owl hoots.
Poets use sound words so that we can 'hear' the poem in our mind.
Sound words are often repeated: tick-tock, pitter-patter, ding-dong.

example.q: Read this poem: Tinkle, tinkle, says my cycle bell, / Ding-dong, ding-dong, the school bells tell. / Jingle, jingle, my ghungroos sing, / Clang, clang, the big brass bells ring! Question: Which sound word does the poet use for the cycle bell?
steps: Find the line about the cycle bell: 'Tinkle, tinkle, says my cycle bell'.
The word that copies the sound is 'tinkle'.
example.answer: tinkle

learn.reallife: Listen at home: the pressure cooker whistles, the tap goes drip-drip and hot oil sizzles when puris go in.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sound word?
quiz.explain: 'Buzz' sounds like the noise a bee makes.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what a sound word is

quiz.q: Poem line: "Clang, clang, the big brass bells ring!" Which word is the sound word?
quiz.explain: 'Clang' copies the loud sound of a big bell.
quiz.mistake: Picks a describing word instead of the sound word

quiz.q: What sound does a snake make?
quiz.explain: A snake makes a hissing sound: hiss!
quiz.mistake: Mixes up animal sounds

quiz.q: Which sound word fits light rain falling on a roof?
quiz.explain: Pitter-patter is the soft, quick sound of raindrops.
quiz.mistake: Picks an animal sound for rain

quiz.q: Poem line: "Jingle, jingle, my ghungroos sing." What makes the jingle sound?
quiz.explain: The line says the ghungroos sing 'jingle, jingle'.
quiz.mistake: Does not match the sound word with its line

quiz.q: Which animal says 'quack'?
quiz.explain: A duck quacks.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up animal sounds

quiz.q: Hot oil when puris go into the kadhai makes which sound?
quiz.explain: Hot oil sizzles when something is put in it.
quiz.mistake: Picks an animal or insect sound

quiz.q: Fill in: "A stone fell into the pond with a ___."
quiz.explain: A stone falling into water makes a splash.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about what sound water makes

teach.ask: Gappu read 'tinkle, tinkle' and 'buzz' in a poem. Why does a poet use words like these?
teach.praise: Yes! Sound words sound like the noise they name, so we can hear the poem in our head. Tweet tweet, says Gappu!
teach.nudge: What do words like tinkle and buzz copy?

learn.hook: Bell, tell, shell, well... why do these words sound so good together?
points: Rhyming words end with the same sound: bell and tell, sing and ring.
Rhyming words do not need to start with the same letter: 'sing' and 'ring' still rhyme.
Rhythm is the beat of a poem. You can clap or tap along to it.
Each beat in a word is called a syllable. Clap 'jin-gle': 2 beats.
Repeating words like 'tinkle, tinkle' adds to the rhythm.

example.q: Think it through: in 'Tinkle, tinkle, says my cycle bell, / Ding-dong, ding-dong, the school bells tell,' which words rhyme?
steps: Look at the last word of each line: 'bell' and 'tell'.
Both end with the sound '-ell'.
So 'bell' and 'tell' rhyme.
example.answer: bell and tell

learn.reallife: Many nursery rhymes and film songs use rhyme and a strong beat. That is why they are easy to remember!

games.title: Which word does it rhyme with?
Rhyme and rhythm: true or false?
items: Rhyming words must start with the same letter.
Rhyming words end with the same sound, like 'sing' and 'ring'.
Clapping can help you feel the rhythm of a poem.
Clap it: ba-na-na. It has three beats.

quiz.q: Which word rhymes with 'bell'?
quiz.explain: 'Shell' ends with the same '-ell' sound as 'bell'.
quiz.mistake: Thinks words that start the same will rhyme

quiz.q: Which pair of words rhymes?
quiz.explain: 'Sing' and 'ring' both end with '-ing'.
quiz.mistake: Looks only at the first letters

quiz.q: Clap the word 'tinkle'. How many beats does it have?
quiz.explain: tin-kle: 2 claps, so 2 beats.
quiz.mistake: Counts letters instead of beats

quiz.q: Clap the word 'butterfly'. How many beats does it have?
quiz.explain: but-ter-fly: 3 claps, so 3 beats.
quiz.mistake: Joins two beats together while clapping

quiz.q: Which word rhymes with 'neck'?
quiz.explain: 'Neck' and 'check' both end with '-eck'.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word that starts with the same sound

quiz.q: What is the rhythm of a poem?
options: The beat you can clap to
quiz.explain: Rhythm is the beat of a poem.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up rhythm and rhyme or the title

quiz.q: Which word does NOT rhyme with 'play'?
quiz.explain: 'Plan' ends in '-an'. The others end in '-ay'.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'plan' rhymes because it starts like 'play'

quiz.q: Why does a poet write "Jingle, jingle" twice in one line?
options: To make a sound and a beat
quiz.explain: Repeating the sound word makes us hear the bells and adds to the rhythm.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that repetition is used on purpose in poems

teach.ask: Gappu says 'bell' and 'tell' sound like friends. What are rhyming words, and what is rhythm?
teach.praise: Correct! Rhyming words end with the same sound, and rhythm is the beat you can clap to. Gappu is clapping his wings!
teach.nudge: What is the same about the ends of 'bell' and 'tell'? And what can you clap to in a poem?

learn.hook: A bell, or a tiny, shiny, golden bell? Describing words make pictures in our mind!
points: An adjective is a describing word. It tells us more about a noun.
Adjectives can tell what kind (sweet, loud), what colour (golden), what size (tiny) or how many (two).
An adjective often comes before a noun: a shiny bell.
It can also come after 'is' or 'are': The bell is shiny.
Many adjectives have opposites: loud and soft, big and small, hot and cold.

example.q: Think it through: find the adjectives in 'The tiny silver bell made a sweet sound.'
steps: Ask: what kind of bell? 'tiny' and 'silver'.
Ask: what kind of sound? 'sweet'.
These three words describe nouns.
example.answer: tiny, silver, sweet

learn.reallife: When you tell your friend about a 'big, red kite' or 'hot, crispy samosas', you are using adjectives.

items.text: The ___ sun shone in the sky.
The bell made a ___ sound.
A snail moves in a ___ way.
I have ___ hands.

quiz.q: Which word is an adjective in "The loud bell woke the baby"?
quiz.explain: 'Loud' describes the bell, so it is an adjective.
quiz.mistake: Picks the noun instead of the word that describes it

quiz.q: "Grandma wore three green bangles." Which word tells how many?
quiz.explain: 'Three' tells us the number of bangles.
quiz.mistake: Picks the colour word instead of the number word

quiz.q: Which adjective is the opposite of 'loud'?
quiz.explain: A loud sound is the opposite of a soft sound.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word that means nearly the same as loud

quiz.q: Which word best describes the taste of a lemon?
quiz.explain: A lemon tastes sour. 'Sour' is an adjective.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word that is not a describing word

quiz.q: Which sentence has an adjective in it?
quiz.explain: 'Juicy' describes the mango.
quiz.mistake: Does not look for a describing word

quiz.q: "The bell is shiny." Which word describes the bell?
quiz.explain: 'Shiny' tells us what the bell is like.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the adjective must come before the noun

quiz.q: Fill in: "Ice cream is ___."
quiz.explain: Ice cream is cold.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about the meaning of the describing word

quiz.q: Which word is NOT an adjective?
quiz.explain: 'Jump' is an action word (verb). The others describe nouns.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up action words and describing words

teach.ask: Gappu has a bell. How can Gappu use adjectives to tell you more about it?
teach.praise: Lovely! An adjective describes a noun, like a 'tiny, golden bell'. Gappu's bell sounds beautiful now!
teach.nudge: What does an adjective do to a noun? Give Gappu one describing word for his bell.

learn.hook: Superheroes are not the only ones who can stay safe. Smart children can too!
points: The lesson 'Be Smart, Be Safe' teaches us simple ways to keep ourselves safe.
On the road, cross at a zebra crossing. In India, look right, then left, then right again.
At home, never touch switches with wet hands, and stay away from a hot stove.
Your body belongs to you. If any touch makes you feel uncomfortable, say 'No' and tell a trusted adult.
A trusted adult is a grown-up who keeps you safe, like a parent, grandparent or teacher.

example.q: Read: Kavya walked to school with her father. At the zebra crossing, they stopped. They looked right, then left, then right again. Only when the road was clear did they cross. "Safety first, always!" said Kavya with a smile. Question: What did Kavya and her father do before crossing?
steps: Find the line just before they crossed.
'They looked right, then left, then right again.'
They crossed only when the road was clear.
example.answer: They stopped and looked right, left and right again, and crossed only when the road was clear.

learn.reallife: Use these safety rules on your way to school, in the park and at home every single day.

games.title: Crossing the road safely
items: Cross when the road is clear

games.title: Safe or not?
items: Touching a switch with wet hands is safe.
Water and electricity together are dangerous. Dry your hands first.
You should cross the road at a zebra crossing.
A zebra crossing is the safe place for people to cross.
If a touch makes you uncomfortable, you can say 'No' and tell a trusted adult.
Your body belongs to you. A trusted adult will help.
A trusted adult is someone who keeps you safe.
Parents, grandparents and teachers are trusted adults.
It is fine to play near a hot stove.
A hot stove can burn you. Stay away from it.

quiz.q: Story line: "At the zebra crossing, they stopped." Where did Kavya and her father stop?
quiz.explain: The line says they stopped at the zebra crossing.
quiz.mistake: Does not find the place word in the line

quiz.q: Story line: "Only when the road was clear did they cross." When did they cross?
quiz.explain: They waited until no vehicles were coming.
quiz.mistake: Thinks people should cross whenever they are in a hurry

quiz.q: Kavya said, "Safety first, always!" What does she mean?
options: She wants to be first in class
Being safe is the most important thing
quiz.explain: 'Safety first' means we should think about being safe before anything else.
quiz.mistake: Takes the word 'first' to mean winning a race

quiz.q: Which is the safe way to cross a road in India?
options: Look right, left, then right again
quiz.explain: In India vehicles drive on the left, so traffic near you comes from the right first.
quiz.mistake: Thinks running fast is safe

quiz.q: Which of these is a safe habit at home?
options: Drying your hands before touching a switch
Putting a pin into a plug socket
quiz.explain: Dry hands keep us safe from electric shock.
quiz.mistake: Does not know which actions are dangerous

quiz.q: Who is a trusted adult?
quiz.explain: A trusted adult is someone you know well who keeps you safe.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a friendly face makes someone trustworthy

quiz.q: A touch makes Riya feel uncomfortable. What should she do?
options: Say 'No' and tell a trusted adult
quiz.explain: Riya should say no and tell a trusted adult. It is never the child's fault.
quiz.mistake: Thinks such things must be kept secret

quiz.q: Which word in "Be smart, be safe" means 'clever'?
quiz.explain: 'Smart' means clever or wise.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of 'smart'

teach.ask: Gappu wants to fly across a busy road and play near the stove. How can Gappu stay safe?
teach.praise: Smart Gappu! Look right, left and right again, stay away from danger and tell a trusted adult if something feels wrong.
teach.nudge: What should Gappu do at a road? And who should Gappu tell if something feels wrong?

learn.hook: Not every stranger is bad, but smart children know the safety rules. Do you?
points: A stranger is a person you do not know.
Never go anywhere with a stranger, even if they offer sweets, toys or a ride.
Remember 'No, Go, Tell': say No loudly, Go away to a safe place, Tell a trusted adult.
Do not share your name, address, school or photos with people you meet online.
Learn a parent's phone number. In an emergency in India, an adult can call 112. The child helpline is 1098.

example.q: Read: After school, Dev waited at the gate for his mother. A man he did not know said, "Your mother is busy. Come with me, I have chocolates." Dev said a loud "No!" He went back inside and told his teacher. His teacher called his mother, who came soon. Question: Did Dev do the right thing? Why?
steps: The man was a stranger to Dev.
Dev said 'No' loudly, went back inside the school and told his teacher.
That is 'No, Go, Tell'.
example.answer: Yes. He said No, went to a safe place and told a trusted adult.

learn.reallife: If you are ever lost in a market or mall, stay where you are, or ask a police officer or a shopkeeper at the counter for help.

games.title: No, Go, Tell
games.prompt: What should you do if a stranger asks you to come along?
items: Go away to a safe place

games.title: Safe or unsafe?
items: Telling your teacher about a stranger
Staying with your group on a school trip
Going with a stranger for sweets
Opening the door to someone you do not know

quiz.q: What is a stranger?
options: A person you do not know
quiz.explain: A stranger is someone you do not know.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a stranger means a scary-looking person

quiz.q: Story line: "Come with me, I have chocolates." What did Dev say?
quiz.explain: Dev said a loud 'No!' to the stranger.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is rude to say no to a grown-up

quiz.q: After saying no, where did Dev go?
quiz.explain: Dev went back inside, which was a safe place.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the story line carefully

quiz.q: Whom did Dev tell about the stranger?
quiz.explain: Dev told his teacher, a trusted adult.
quiz.mistake: Thinks telling a friend is enough

quiz.q: What do the words 'No, Go, Tell' remind us to do?
options: Say no, go to a safe place, tell a trusted adult
Go with the stranger and tell later
quiz.explain: These three steps keep us safe from strangers.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order or meaning of the steps

quiz.q: Someone you met in an online game asks for your home address. What should you do?
options: Not share it and tell a parent
Send a photo of your house
quiz.explain: We never share personal details online. Tell a parent or a trusted adult.
quiz.mistake: Thinks online friends are the same as real friends

quiz.q: What is the child helpline number in India?
quiz.explain: 1098 is the child helpline number in India.
quiz.mistake: Mixes it up with other emergency numbers

quiz.q: You are lost in a big market. Who is a good person to ask for help?
options: A person who asks you to come to his car
quiz.explain: A police officer is there to help people who are lost.
quiz.mistake: Does not know who safe helpers are

teach.ask: A stranger tells Gappu, 'Come with me, I have juicy worms!' What should Gappu do?
teach.praise: Perfect! Say No, Go to a safe place and Tell a trusted adult. Gappu will never go with a stranger!
teach.nudge: What three things should Gappu do? Start with what Gappu should say.

learn.hook: "Stop!" "Are you safe?" "What a busy road!" Every sentence has a different job.
points: A statement tells us something. It ends with a full stop (.): I walk to school.
A question asks something. It ends with a question mark (?): Where is your bag?
A command or request tells someone to do something. It ends with a full stop: Look both ways. Please close the door.
An exclamation shows a strong feeling like surprise or joy. It ends with an exclamation mark (!): What a big truck!
Every sentence begins with a capital letter.

example.q: Think it through: what kind of sentence is 'Do not talk to strangers.'?
steps: It does not just tell a fact, and it does not ask anything.
It tells someone what to do (or not do).
So it is a command. It ends with a full stop.
example.answer: A command

learn.reallife: Safety signs use commands like 'Stop', 'Keep left' and 'Do not touch'.

items.text: Is this your pencil___
What a huge elephant___
I have a red bag___
When does the bus come___

quiz.q: Which sentence is a question?
quiz.explain: It asks something and ends with a question mark.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence with 'where' or 'what' is a question

quiz.q: What kind of sentence is "Look both ways before you cross."?
quiz.explain: It tells someone what to do, so it is a command.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every sentence with a full stop is a statement

quiz.q: Which mark should end this sentence: "What a beautiful kite"
quiz.explain: It shows a strong feeling, so it ends with an exclamation mark.
quiz.mistake: Uses a question mark because the sentence starts with 'What'

quiz.q: Which sentence is a statement?
quiz.explain: It tells us a fact and ends with a full stop.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what a statement is

quiz.q: Which sentence is written correctly?
quiz.explain: It starts with a capital letter and ends with a question mark.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the capital letter or the question mark

quiz.q: What kind of sentence is "Please hold my hand."?
quiz.explain: It asks someone politely to do something. A polite command is a request.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'please' makes it a question

quiz.q: Which sentence shows surprise?
quiz.explain: 'Wow' and the exclamation mark show surprise.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the feeling word and the exclamation mark

quiz.q: Which mark ends a question?
quiz.explain: A question ends with a question mark (?).
quiz.mistake: Mixes up punctuation marks

teach.ask: Gappu wrote 'where is my nest' and does not know how to end it. What kind of sentence is it, and what mark goes at the end?
teach.praise: Well done! It is a question, so it starts with a capital letter and ends with a question mark. Gappu's sentence is perfect now!
teach.nudge: Is Gappu telling, asking or ordering? Which mark goes at the end of an asking sentence?

learn.hook: Can you colour a picture, watch cartoons and eat a samosa all at once? Things can get messy!
points: The poem 'One Thing at a Time' tells us to give our full attention to one task before we start the next.
To focus means to give all your attention to one thing.
When we focus, our work is neater and we finish it faster.
Things that pull our attention away, like a TV that is on, are called distractions.
The poem also says there is a time for work and a time for play.

example.q: Read this poem: When I draw, I only draw, / I do not watch TV. / When I read, I only read, / The words come clear to me. / When work is done, I run to play, / And laugh the whole bright day! Question: What does the child do after the work is done?
steps: Find the line that begins 'When work is done'.
It says 'I run to play'.
So the child plays only after finishing the work.
example.answer: The child runs out to play.

learn.reallife: Switch off the TV while you do homework. You will finish quicker and have more time to play!

games.title: Match the word to its meaning
pairs: something that takes your attention away
a piece of work to do

games.title: Focus: true or false?

A loud TV is a distraction.

The child plays after the work is done.
Focusing means doing five things at once.
Focusing means giving attention to one thing.
Keeping your desk tidy can help you focus.
A tidy desk has fewer things to distract you.

quiz.q: Poem lines: "When I draw, I only draw, / I do not watch TV." What does the child do while drawing?

quiz.mistake: Does not notice the word 'only'

quiz.mistake: Does not link focus with understanding

quiz.explain: The child plays only after the work is finished.

quiz.explain: 'Play' and 'day' end with the same '-ay' sound.

quiz.explain: When you focus, all your attention is on one thing.
quiz.mistake: Thinks focus means doing more things at once

quiz.q: Which child is focusing on the work?
options: Ravi reads while playing a video game
Asha does her sums with the TV off
Meena writes while chatting with a friend
quiz.explain: Asha has no distraction, so she can give full attention to her sums.
quiz.mistake: Thinks doing two things at once is focusing

quiz.q: What is the main message of the poem?
options: Do one thing at a time with full attention
quiz.explain: The poem says to focus on one task and to play after work.
quiz.mistake: Picks one small detail instead of the main idea

quiz.q: Poem line: "And laugh the whole bright day!" How does the child feel?
quiz.explain: Laughing shows the child is happy.
quiz.mistake: Does not use 'laugh' as a clue to feelings

teach.ask: Gappu is eating, singing and doing homework all at once. The homework is a mess! What should Gappu do?
teach.praise: Yes! Do one thing at a time with full focus, and play after the work is done. Gappu's homework will be neat now!
teach.nudge: How many things should Gappu do at one time? And when should Gappu play?

topics.title: Work and play: one and many

learn.hook: One toy, two toys. One box, two... boxs? No! Let us find out the right way.
points: Work like homework and helping at home comes first. Play time is more fun when work is done.
To make most nouns plural (more than one), add -s: toy → toys, book → books.
Add -es to words ending in s, x, ch or sh: bus → buses, box → boxes, watch → watches, brush → brushes.
If a word ends in a consonant + y, change y to i and add -es: story → stories. But day → days, because 'a' comes before y.
Some words change in a special way: child → children, tooth → teeth, foot → feet, mouse → mice, leaf → leaves.

example.q: Think it through: what is the plural of 'hobby'?
steps: 'Hobby' ends in y.
The letter before y is 'b', a consonant.
So change y to i and add -es.
example.answer: hobbies

learn.reallife: Count things in your room: two pencils, three boxes, four brushes. Saying them aloud is plural practice!

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'box'?
quiz.explain: Words ending in x take -es: boxes.
quiz.mistake: Adds only -s to a word ending in x

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'story'?
quiz.explain: Story ends in a consonant + y, so y changes to i and we add -es.
quiz.mistake: Adds -s without changing y

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'child'?
quiz.explain: 'Child' has a special plural: children.
quiz.mistake: Adds -s to every noun

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'leaf'?
quiz.explain: In 'leaf', f changes to v and we add -es: leaves.
quiz.mistake: Adds -s without changing f to v

quiz.q: Fill in: "Ravi packed three ___ into his school bag."
quiz.explain: Three means more than one, so we add -s: books.

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'brush'?
quiz.explain: Words ending in sh take -es: brushes.
quiz.mistake: Adds only -s to a word ending in sh

quiz.q: Which of these is a chore (work) you can do at home?
quiz.explain: Folding clothes is a job that helps at home. The others are games.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up work and play

quiz.q: "Finish your homework first, then go out to play." Why is this a good plan?
options: You never have to do homework

quiz.explain: When the work is finished, you can enjoy playing without worry.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the plan means no play at all

teach.ask: Gappu has one kite and you give him two more. Gappu says 'three kites', but for 'box' he says 'three boxs'. Help Gappu!
teach.praise: Great! For more than one we usually add -s, but words ending in x, s, ch or sh take -es. Three boxes, Gappu!
teach.nudge: What do we add to 'box' to make it more than one?

topics.title: Action words: verbs in the present

learn.hook: Run, read, draw, jump! A sentence cannot work without an action word.
points: A verb is an action word. It tells what someone or something does: run, read, eat, sing.
We use the simple present tense for things we do every day: I play cricket every evening.
With I, you, we and they, the verb stays the same: I play, they play.
With he, she, it or one person's name, add -s: Asha plays. Add -es after s, x, ch, sh or o: watches, goes.
If a verb ends in a consonant + y, change y to i and add -es: fly → flies, cry → cries.

example.q: Think it through: choose the right verb. 'Meena (read / reads) a story every night.'
steps: Meena is one person, so she is like 'she'.
With she, we add -s to the verb.
So we write 'reads'.
example.answer: Meena reads a story every night.

learn.reallife: Tell someone your daily routine: I wake up, I brush my teeth, I go to school. Those are present-tense verbs!

quiz.explain: 'Write' is an action word.
quiz.mistake: Picks a naming or describing word

quiz.explain: With one person (he), 'go' becomes 'goes'.
quiz.mistake: Adds only -s to 'go'

quiz.explain: Cry ends in a consonant + y, so it becomes cries.

quiz.explain: With 'we', the verb stays the same: do.

quiz.explain: Wash ends in sh, so with 'she' it becomes washes.
quiz.mistake: Adds only -s to a word ending in sh

quiz.q: Find the verb in "Kabir paints a big kite."
quiz.explain: 'Paints' tells what Kabir does.

quiz.explain: The cat is 'it', so we add -s: drinks.

quiz.explain: Rohan and Meera are two people (they), so the verb stays 'play'.
quiz.mistake: Adds -s even when there are two people

teach.ask: Gappu says 'Gappu fly every day.' Something is wrong. What is a verb, and how should Gappu say it?
teach.praise: Super! A verb is an action word. For one bird we say 'Gappu flies'. Gappu is flapping happily!
teach.nudge: What kind of word is 'fly'? And how does it change for just one bird?

learn.hook: Why would fast young deer need help from a slow old stag? Read on to find out!
points: 'The Old Stag' is a fable. A stag is a male deer.
A fable is a short story where animals talk and act like people. It teaches a lesson called a moral.
Every story has characters (who), a setting (where and when), a problem and a solution.
India has old collections of fables, like the Panchatantra and the Jataka tales.
To find the moral, ask: what did the characters learn at the end?

example.q: Read this fable: In a forest near the Satpura hills lived an old stag named Dhruv. The young deer laughed, "You are so slow, grandpa!" One hot summer, the ponds dried up. The young deer were thirsty and worried. "Follow me," said Dhruv. He walked slowly to a hidden spring behind the big rocks. "I found it many summers ago," he said. The young deer said, "We are sorry. You are slow, but you are wise." Question: What lesson did the young deer learn?
steps: At first, they laughed at Dhruv for being slow.
When there was no water, Dhruv's old memory saved them.
At the end they said, 'You are slow, but you are wise.'
example.answer: Old people may be slow, but they are wise because of their experience. We should respect them.

learn.reallife: Your grandparents know old recipes, games and stories. Ask them. Their experience is a treasure!

teach.nudge: What do old animals and people have that young ones may not? How should we treat them?

learn.hook: A stag, a doe and a fawn walk into a forest. Who is who?
points: Wisdom means good sense that comes from learning and experience.
A proverb is a short, wise saying: 'Look before you leap' means think carefully before you act.
'Slow and steady wins the race' means working steadily without giving up brings success.
Male and female names: stag – doe, lion – lioness, peacock – peahen, horse – mare, king – queen.
Young ones: deer – fawn, cat – kitten, dog – puppy, hen – chick, sheep – lamb, lion – cub.

example.q: Think it through: what does 'Look before you leap' mean for Riya, who wants to jump into a puddle?
steps: 'Leap' means jump.
'Look before you leap' tells us to check first.
Riya should check how deep or dirty the puddle is before jumping.
example.answer: Think and check carefully before you act.

teach.praise: Correct! The stag is the male deer, the doe is the female deer and the fawn is the baby. Gappu waves at the deer family!
teach.nudge: Which one is the father deer, which is the mother, and which is the baby?

topics.title: Telling the past: past tense verbs

learn.hook: Fables happened 'long, long ago'. So we tell them in the past tense!
points: The past tense tells us about something that has already happened: yesterday, last week, long ago.
Most verbs add -ed: walk → walked, laugh → laughed. If a verb ends in e, add -d: smile → smiled.
Some short verbs double the last letter: stop → stopped, hop → hopped.
If a verb ends in a consonant + y, change y to i and add -ed: cry → cried, dry → dried.
Some verbs change completely: go → went, see → saw, eat → ate, find → found, drink → drank, say → said.

example.q: Think it through: change to the past: 'The old stag finds a spring.'
steps: The verb is 'finds'.
'Find' does not take -ed. Its past form is special.
find → found
example.answer: The old stag found a spring.

learn.reallife: When you tell your family about your day at school, you use the past tense: I played, I ate, I learnt.

quiz.explain: 'Go' is a special verb. Its past tense is 'went'.

quiz.q: Which word in "Last week, we visited the zoo" is a verb in the past tense?

teach.ask: Gappu says, 'Yesterday I goed to the river and eated a worm.' Can you help Gappu fix it?

topics.title: Louis Braille: the boy who made dots talk

learn.hook: Can you read a book with your eyes closed? A teenage boy found a way!
points: The lesson 'Braille' tells the story of Louis Braille and his gift to the world.
Louis Braille was born in France in 1809. He lost his sight in an accident when he was a small child.
At his school in Paris, there were very few books that blind students could read.
As a teenager, he made a reading and writing system of raised dots. We call it braille.
World Braille Day is on 4 January, his birthday.

example.q: Read: Louis Braille was born in France in 1809. When he was a small child, an accident hurt his eyes, and he lost his sight. At a school for blind children in Paris, he found very few books he could read. So, when he was only about fifteen, he made a new way of reading with raised dots. Today, people all over the world use braille. Question: Why did Louis Braille make a new way of reading?
steps: Find the line about his school: 'he found very few books he could read.'
He wanted blind people to read easily.
So he made a system of raised dots.
example.answer: Because there were very few books that blind children like him could read.

learn.reallife: Look out for braille dots on lift buttons, some medicine boxes and signs in railway stations and airports.

learn.hook: Close your eyes and touch a coin. Can you feel its edges? Your fingers can 'see' too!
points: Braille is a code for reading and writing. It is not a separate language.

topics.title: Everyone belongs: inclusion and word beginnings

learn.hook: Ramps, braille signs and kind friends: they help everyone join in!
points: Inclusion means making sure everyone can take part, whatever their abilities.
Ramps, braille signs, talking books and sign language help people join in.
We use kind, respectful words. We say 'a person who is blind' or 'visually impaired'.
A prefix is added at the start of a word to change its meaning: un + kind = unkind.
un-, dis- and im- often mean 'not': unable, unfair, dislike, disagree, impossible, impolite.

example.q: Think it through: Louis Braille showed that reading without sight was not im___. Which word fits?
steps: 'Possible' means it can happen.
The prefix 'im-' means 'not'.
So 'impossible' means it cannot happen. Louis showed it was possible!
example.answer: impossible

learn.reallife: In your class, you can include everyone: pick a new friend for your team, or help a classmate read the board.

chapters.title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation

learn.hook: Can you stand like a mountain and balance like a tree? Yoga lets you try!
points: The lesson 'Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation' says that fit, healthy people make a strong country.
Being fit means having a strong, healthy body and a calm, happy mind.
Running, skipping, cycling, swimming and outdoor games keep us fit.
Yoga is an old Indian practice of body poses (asanas), slow breathing and relaxing.
International Day of Yoga is celebrated every year on 21 June.

example.q: Read: Every morning, Anaya and her grandfather do yoga on the terrace in Pune. First they stand tall like a mountain in Tadasana. Then they balance on one leg like a tree in Vrikshasana. They breathe in slowly and breathe out slowly. "Now my body feels strong and my mind feels calm," says Anaya. Question: How does yoga help Anaya?
steps: Find what Anaya says at the end.
'Now my body feels strong and my mind feels calm.'
So yoga helps both her body and her mind.
example.answer: It makes her body feel strong and her mind feel calm.

learn.reallife: Try stretching for a few minutes every morning with a grown-up. Learn new poses only from a teacher or an adult who knows yoga.

learn.hook: A habit is something you do again and again. Is your habit helpful or harmful?
points: Healthy habits: eat fruits and vegetables, drink clean water, sleep on time and play outdoors.
Wash your hands with soap before eating, and brush your teeth twice a day.
Too much junk food and screen time are not good for us.
The suffix '-ful' means 'full of': help + ful = helpful, care + ful = careful.
The suffix '-less' means 'without': care + less = careless, harm + less = harmless.

example.q: Think it through: 'Eating only junk food every day can be ___ for your body.' Is it 'harmful' or 'harmless'?
steps: 'Harmful' means full of harm. 'Harmless' means without harm.
Too much junk food is bad for the body.
So the right word is 'harmful'.
example.answer: harmful

learn.hook: Do you breathe quickly or slowly in yoga? The answer is an adverb!
points: An adverb tells us more about a verb (an action word).
Some adverbs tell HOW: slowly, quickly, gently, loudly, carefully.
Some adverbs tell WHEN: today, now, early, tomorrow. Some tell WHERE: outside, here, there.
Many 'how' adverbs are made by adding -ly to an adjective: slow → slowly, quick → quickly.
If the word ends in y, change y to i: happy → happily, easy → easily.

example.q: Think it through: find the adverb in 'Anaya breathes slowly.'
steps: The verb is 'breathes'.
Ask: how does she breathe? Slowly.
'Slowly' tells us more about the verb, so it is an adverb.

quiz.mistake: Picks the verb instead of the place word

learn.hook: All you need is a ball, some flat stones and your friends. Ready for lagori?
points: 'The Lagori Champions' is about children who play lagori, a traditional Indian game.
Lagori is played with a ball and a pile of flat stones.
It has other names too. In many places it is called pitthu.
Two teams play. One team knocks down the pile with the ball and tries to build it again. The other team tries to get them out with the ball.
Lagori needs good aim, quick feet and teamwork.

example.q: Read: It was the inter-school lagori match in Hubballi. Team Sunflower threw the ball and knocked down the pile of seven flat stones. Quickly, they began to stack the stones again. Team Mango tried to get them out with the ball. Just in time, Leela placed the last stone and shouted, "Lagori!" Team Sunflower won. Team Mango clapped and said, "Well played!" Question: How did Team Sunflower win?
steps: Team Sunflower knocked down the pile.
They stacked the stones again while Team Mango tried to get them out.
Leela placed the last stone just in time and shouted 'Lagori!'
example.answer: They rebuilt the pile of stones before Team Mango could get them out.

learn.hook: Team Mango lost, but they still clapped. Why do you think they did that?
points: A good sport plays fair and follows the rules.
A good sport is kind whether they win or lose. They say 'Well played!' to the other team.
A good sport helps a player who falls and respects the umpire or referee.
Useful words: opponent (the team you play against), captain (team leader), champion (winner), cheer (shout to encourage).
Opposites: win – lose, fair – unfair, start – finish.

example.q: Think it through: Team Mango lost the match but clapped and said 'Well played!' What does this show?
steps: Losing can make you feel sad.
Even so, they praised the winners.
Being kind to the other team after losing is sportsmanship.
example.answer: It shows good sportsmanship.

learn.reallife: In school sports day, cheer for every runner, not just your friends. Shake hands after a match.

learn.hook: Leela placed the stone. Leela shouted. Can one little word join these sentences?
points: A conjunction is a joining word. It joins words or sentences.
'and' adds things together: I like kabaddi and kho-kho.
'but' shows something different or surprising: We were tired, but we kept playing.
'or' gives a choice: Do you want a ball or a bat?
'because' gives a reason, and 'so' gives a result: We won because we worked together. It was dark, so we went home.

example.q: Think it through: join 'Leela placed the last stone.' and 'Leela shouted "Lagori!"'
steps: Both sentences tell what Leela did, one after another.
We are adding one action to another.
So we use 'and'.
example.answer: Leela placed the last stone and shouted "Lagori!"

learn.reallife: You use conjunctions all the time: 'Can I go out and play? I finished my homework, so I am free!'

topics.title: Reading: a quiet morning in nature

learn.hook: Sit still for one minute outside. How many living things can you spot?
points: 'Hekko' is a lesson set in nature. It invites us to look closely at the world around us.
Nature includes plants, animals, birds, insects, rain, soil and sky.
When we are quiet and patient, we notice small things, like ants or a snail.
Writers use our senses to describe nature: what we see, hear, smell and feel.
To answer a question about a passage, find the exact line that has the answer.

example.q: Read: Early one morning, Tara sat quietly under a neem tree in her village in Odisha. She watched a line of ants carrying tiny crumbs. She heard a bulbul singing on a branch. She smelt the wet earth after the rain. A small snail was moving slowly on a leaf. "If I sit still and look closely," Tara thought, "nature shows me so much!" Question: Which things did Tara notice by seeing?
steps: Look for the words 'watched' and things she saw.
She watched the ants carrying crumbs.
She also saw the snail moving on a leaf.

topics.title: Looking closely: sense words and sound-alike words

learn.hook: You can 'see' the sea and 'hear' a bird right here. Wait, what?
points: Observation means looking, listening and noticing carefully.
We use five senses: see (eyes), hear (ears), smell (nose), taste (tongue) and touch (skin).
Touch words: rough, smooth, prickly. Taste words: sweet, sour, salty, bitter.
A magnifying glass helps us observe tiny details, like the veins on a leaf.
Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings: see – sea, hear – here, sun – son, flour – flower.

example.q: Think it through: 'We went to ___ the ___.' Which pair goes in: see or sea?
steps: 'See' means to look with your eyes.
'Sea' is a big body of salty water.
We go to look at the water, so: We went to see the sea.

learn.reallife: On a walk, play 'I spy' with your family. It trains you to observe!

quiz.explain: A magnifying glass makes small things look bigger so we can observe them.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a magnifying glass really changes the object

teach.ask: Gappu wrote 'I can here a bird.' Is that right? Explain to Gappu.
teach.praise: Correct! It should be 'hear', because we hear with our ears. 'Here' means this place. They are homophones! Gappu fixed it.
teach.nudge: Which spelling is about listening with ears? What do we call words that sound the same?

learn.hook: The snail is ON the leaf. The ant is UNDER the stone. Little words tell us where things are!
points: A preposition tells us where something is, or its position.
Common prepositions: in, on, under, behind, between, above, near, in front of.
'in' means inside: The fish is in the pond. 'on' means on top of: The snail is on the leaf.
'between' means in the middle of two things: B comes between A and C.
'above' means higher than: The kite is above the trees.

example.q: Think it through: 'Tara sat ___ the neem tree.' Which preposition fits: under, between or into?
steps: Tara is below the branches of the tree.
'Between' needs two things, and 'into' shows going inside.
'Under' shows she is below the tree.
example.answer: Tara sat under the neem tree.

learn.reallife: When you help find Dadi's glasses, you use prepositions: 'They are on the table, behind the radio!'

items.text: The fish swims ___ the pond.
The snail is ___ the leaf.
The letter B comes ___ A and C.
The kite flew high ___ the trees.
Dev hid ___ the door during hide and seek.

games.title: Prepositions: true or false?
items: A preposition tells us where something is.
Words like in, on and under show position.
It shows that something is below something else.
In 'The book is on the table', the preposition is 'book'.
'On' is the preposition. 'Book' is a noun.
'Between' is used for something in the middle of two things.
For example: I sat between Ravi and Asha.

quiz.q: Which word is a preposition?
quiz.explain: 'Under' tells us position.
quiz.mistake: Picks a noun, verb or adjective

quiz.q: Fill in: "The cat is hiding ___ the sofa."
quiz.explain: 'Behind' means at the back of. The cat is at the back of the sofa.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'between', which needs two things

quiz.explain: A fish swims inside the water, so we use 'in'.

quiz.q: Fill in: "Riya sat ___ her two friends."
quiz.explain: She is in the middle of two friends, so we use 'between'.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that 'two' needs 'between'

quiz.q: Fill in: "The bird's nest is high ___ the ground."
quiz.explain: The nest is higher than the ground, so we use 'above'.

quiz.q: Which is the preposition in "The bulbul sat on the branch"?
quiz.explain: 'On' tells us where the bulbul sat.
quiz.mistake: Picks the noun or the verb

quiz.explain: The books go inside the bag, so we use 'in'.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about where the books go

quiz.q: What does 'in front of' mean?
quiz.explain: 'In front of' means ahead of something, at its front side. 'Behind' is its opposite.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'in front of' and 'behind'

teach.ask: Gappu lost his worm. You can see it below a stone. How can you use a preposition to tell Gappu where it is?
teach.praise: Super! 'The worm is under the stone.' 'Under' is a preposition. It tells where. Gappu found his breakfast!
teach.nudge: Which word tells Gappu where the worm is? What do we call such words?

topics.title: Reading a poem about a swing

learn.hook: Whoosh! Forward and back, up and down. What does it feel like to fly on a swing?
points: 'The Swing' is a poem about the joy of swinging high in the air.
A poem is written in lines. A group of lines is called a stanza.
Poems often have rhyming words at the ends of lines.
The person who writes a poem is called a poet.
Poets help us imagine: a swing can make us feel like we are flying.

example.q: Read this poem: Under the banyan, my swing hangs low, / Didi gives a push and away I go! / Forward I fly with my toes to the sun, / Back I come laughing, oh, what fun! / The parrots cheer and the breezes sing, / My heart flies high on my happy swing! Question: Which words rhyme with 'go', 'sun' and 'swing'?
steps: Look at the last word of each pair of lines.
low – go, sun – fun, sing – swing.
So 'low' rhymes with 'go', 'fun' with 'sun' and 'sing' with 'swing'.
example.answer: low, fun and sing

learn.reallife: Next time you are on a swing in the park, say a rhyme to the beat of your swing!

games.title: Poem lines in order

My heart flies high on my happy swing!

Poems are made of lines, and lines are grouped into stanzas.
The person who writes a poem is called a poet.

quiz.explain: The line says the swing hangs under the banyan.

quiz.explain: The line says Didi gives a push.
quiz.mistake: Guesses instead of reading the line

quiz.explain: The line begins 'Forward I fly'.

quiz.explain: The child is laughing and says 'what fun!'
quiz.mistake: Does not use 'laughing' and 'fun' as clues

quiz.q: Poem lines: "The parrots cheer and the breezes sing, My heart flies high on my happy swing!" Which word rhymes with 'swing'?
quiz.explain: 'Sing' and 'swing' both end with '-ing'.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word from the poem that does not rhyme

quiz.q: Poem line: "The parrots cheer and the breezes sing," Who cheers?
quiz.explain: The line says 'The parrots cheer'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the parrots and the breezes

quiz.q: In a poem, one row of words is called a ___.
quiz.explain: Each row of words in a poem is a line.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the parts of a poem

quiz.q: What is a group of lines in a poem called?
quiz.explain: A group of lines in a poem is a stanza. A paragraph is used in stories, not poems.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up stanza and paragraph

teach.ask: Gappu read a poem but does not know what a line, a stanza and a poet are. Can you explain?
teach.praise: Brilliant! A line is one row, a stanza is a group of lines, and a poet writes the poem. Gappu wants to write a poem now!
teach.nudge: What is one row of a poem called? And a group of lines? Who writes poems?

topics.title: The joy of play: feeling words and opposites

learn.hook: Up, down, forward, back! A swing is full of opposites, and full of joy!
points: Play makes us happy and healthy and helps us make friends.
Feeling words: happy, joyful, cheerful, excited, thrilled. Thrilled means very happy and excited.
Unhappy feeling words: sad, bored, upset, gloomy.
A swing shows many opposites: up – down, high – low, forward – backward, push – pull.
When we take turns on the swing, everyone gets to play.

example.q: Think it through: 'Riya could not wait for her turn on the swing.' Which feeling word fits Riya: excited or bored?
steps: 'Could not wait' means she really wanted her turn.
A bored person does not care.
So Riya is excited.
example.answer: excited

learn.reallife: At the park, count how many children are waiting. Taking turns makes play fun for all.

quiz.q: Which word means the same as 'happy'?
quiz.explain: 'Joyful' is a synonym of 'happy'.
quiz.mistake: Picks an opposite instead of a synonym

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'push'?
quiz.explain: We push to move something away and pull to bring it towards us.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word that means nearly the same as push

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'high'?
quiz.explain: 'Low' is the opposite of 'high'.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word linked with high

quiz.q: "Riya could not wait for her turn on the swing." How did Riya feel?
quiz.explain: 'Could not wait' shows she was excited.
quiz.mistake: Does not understand the phrase 'could not wait'

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'forward'?
quiz.explain: 'Backward' is the opposite of 'forward'.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word with a similar meaning

quiz.q: Why is outdoor play good for children?
options: It is bad for our eyes
It keeps us healthy and happy
quiz.explain: Running, swinging and playing make our body strong and our mind happy.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the benefits of play

quiz.q: Children are taking turns on the swing. What does this show?
quiz.explain: Taking turns is fair and lets everyone play.
quiz.mistake: Does not see turn-taking as sharing

quiz.q: Which word means 'very happy and excited'?
quiz.explain: Thrilled means very happy and excited.
quiz.mistake: Picks an unhappy feeling word

teach.ask: Gappu sat on a swing for the first time. How might Gappu feel, and what opposites can Gappu feel on a swing?
teach.praise: Yes! Gappu feels joyful and excited, going up and down, forward and backward. Those are opposites! Wheee!
teach.nudge: What is one happy feeling word? And what is the opposite of 'up'?

topics.title: Words that take a noun's place: pronouns

learn.hook: 'Didi pushed Didi's swing and Didi laughed.' Too many Didis! Let us fix it.
points: A pronoun takes the place of a noun so we do not repeat it.
Didi → she, Arjun → he, the swing → it, Riya and I → we, the children → they.
Before the verb (doing the action) we use: I, you, he, she, it, we, they.
After the verb or after words like 'to' and 'with' we use: me, you, him, her, it, us, them.
The pronoun 'I' is always written as a capital letter.

example.q: Think it through: replace the repeated nouns: 'Didi pushed Didi's swing and Didi laughed.'
steps: Didi is a girl, so we use 'she' for the one doing the action.
For something that belongs to her, we use 'her'.
Didi pushed her swing and she laughed.
example.answer: Didi pushed her swing and she laughed.

learn.reallife: When you talk about your friends, you use pronouns all the time: 'She is my best friend. We play together.'

items.text: Arjun loves the swing. ___ swings every evening.

Riya and I are friends. ___ play together.
Please play with ___.
The parrots sang because ___ were happy.

quiz.q: Fill in: "Didi pushed the swing. ___ pushed it high."
quiz.explain: Didi is a girl, so we use 'She'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'he' for a girl

quiz.q: Fill in: "Arjun and I went to the park. ___ played on the swing."
quiz.explain: Arjun and I together are 'we'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'they' when the speaker is included

quiz.q: Fill in: "Please give the ball to ___."
quiz.explain: After 'to' we use 'me', not 'I'.
quiz.mistake: Uses the doer form 'I' after 'to'

quiz.q: Which word is a pronoun?
quiz.explain: 'They' takes the place of a noun.
quiz.mistake: Picks a noun or a verb

quiz.q: Fill in: "The parrots cheered. ___ were happy."
quiz.explain: Parrots are many, so we use 'They'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'it' for more than one

quiz.q: Which sentence is correct?
quiz.explain: The doers of the action take 'I', so we say 'Mohan and I went home.'
quiz.mistake: Uses 'me' or 'him' for the doer

quiz.q: Fill in: "Grandpa called Ravi and Asha. He gave ___ some laddoos."
quiz.explain: Ravi and Asha receive the laddoos, so after the verb we use 'them'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'they' after the verb

quiz.q: Which pronoun is always written with a capital letter?
quiz.explain: The pronoun 'I' is always a capital letter.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all pronouns need capitals

teach.ask: Gappu says, 'Gappu likes the swing. Gappu swings and Gappu sings.' That is a lot of Gappu! How can pronouns help?
teach.praise: Perfect! 'Gappu likes the swing. He swings and he sings.' A pronoun takes the place of a noun. Gappu sounds much better!
teach.nudge: Which word can we use instead of 'Gappu'? What do we call such words?

chapters.title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains

learn.hook: Tunnels, bridges and snowy peaks! Shall we hop on a little mountain train?
points: 'A Journey to the Magical Mountains' is a travel story about a trip to the mountains.
A travel story tells us where people went, how they travelled and what they saw.
Writers use describing words to help us picture places: snowy peaks, tall pine trees.
Mountains are often cold, especially at night and in winter.
The words 'first', 'then', 'far away' and 'that night' help us follow the journey.

example.q: Read: In May, Ishaan's family took the toy train from Kalka to Shimla. The little train puffed through tunnels and over bridges. Pine trees stood tall on the slopes. Far away, Ishaan saw snowy peaks shining in the sun. "The mountains look magical!" he gasped. That night, it was so cold that he slept under two warm quilts. Question: How did Ishaan travel, and what did he see?
steps: Find how they travelled: 'took the toy train from Kalka to Shimla'.
Find what he saw: tunnels, bridges, pine trees and snowy peaks.
Put the two answers together.
example.answer: He travelled by toy train and saw tunnels, bridges, pine trees and snowy peaks.

learn.reallife: When you go on a trip, write a short travel diary: where you went, how you went and the best thing you saw.

quiz.q: Story line: "That night, it was so cold that he slept under two warm quilts." Why did he use two quilts?
quiz.explain: The night was so cold that he needed two quilts.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the quilts with the cold

quiz.q: Story line: "In May, Ishaan's family took the toy train." In which month was the trip?
quiz.explain: The story begins 'In May'.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a cold month because of the snow

quiz.q: What is a travel story about?
quiz.explain: A travel story tells about a journey and what people saw.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what a travel story is

teach.ask: Gappu wants to write a travel story about flying to the hills. What should Gappu put in it?
teach.praise: Super! A travel story tells where you went, how you travelled and what you saw and felt. Gappu's story will be magical!
teach.nudge: What three things should a travel story tell us?

learn.hook: Peaks, valleys, glaciers and plateaus: Earth has so many shapes of land!
points: A mountain is very high land. Its top is called the peak, and its sides are slopes.
A valley is low land between hills or mountains. Rivers often flow through valleys.
A glacier is a huge mass of ice that moves very slowly.
A plateau is high, flat land. A plain is wide, flat, low land. An island is land with water all around it.
The Himalayas are in the north of India. Mount Everest, the highest mountain in the world, is in the Himalayas.

example.q: Think it through: Ishaan stands on a mountain and looks down at a low area with a river between two mountains. What is it called?
steps: It is low land.
It lies between mountains.
Low land between hills or mountains is a valley.
example.answer: A valley

learn.reallife: India has every kind of land: the Himalayas, the Ganga plains, the Thar Desert, the Deccan Plateau and islands like the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

games.title: Match the landform
pairs: a huge, slow-moving mass of ice

quiz.explain: The highest point of a mountain is its peak.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the parts of a mountain

quiz.q: What do we call low land between hills or mountains?
quiz.explain: A valley is low land between hills or mountains.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up valley and plateau

teach.praise: Correct! The pointy top is a peak, the low land is a valley and the high flat land is a plateau. Gappu is a geography star!
teach.nudge: What is the top of a mountain called? And the low land between mountains?

learn.hook: A hill is high. A mountain is higher. Mount Everest is the highest! How do words change when we compare?
points: To compare two things, add -er and use 'than': This hill is taller than that hill.
To compare three or more, use 'the' and add -est: Everest is the tallest of all.
Short words ending in one vowel + consonant double the last letter: big → bigger → biggest.
Words ending in y change y to i: happy → happier → happiest.
Long words use more and most: beautiful → more beautiful → most beautiful. Special ones: good → better → best, bad → worse → worst.

example.q: Think it through: 'Of all the peaks, Everest is the ___.' (high)
steps: We are comparing many peaks, not just two.
So we use 'the' and add -est.
high → highest
example.answer: Of all the peaks, Everest is the highest.

learn.reallife: You compare every day: 'My brother is taller than me. Mango is the best fruit!'

quiz.explain: Comparing two things: big → bigger (double the g).
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the last letter

quiz.q: Fill in: "Of the three peaks, this one is the ___." (tall)
quiz.explain: Comparing three or more: tallest.
quiz.mistake: Uses -er when comparing more than two

quiz.q: Which word compares two things using 'good'?
quiz.explain: good → better → best. 'Better' compares two.
quiz.mistake: Adds -er to a special word

quiz.q: Fill in: "The valley is ___ than the town." (beautiful)
quiz.explain: Long words use 'more' to compare two things.
quiz.mistake: Adds -er to a long word

quiz.q: Which word means 'the most bad'?
quiz.explain: bad → worse → worst.
quiz.mistake: Adds -est to a special word

quiz.q: Fill in: "Today is ___ than yesterday." (cold)
quiz.explain: Comparing two days: colder.
quiz.mistake: Uses -est when comparing only two

quiz.q: Fill in: "Ishaan was the ___ child on the train." (happy)
quiz.explain: Comparing him with all the children: change y to i and add -est.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change y to i

quiz.q: Fill in: "A glacier moves ___ than a river." (slow)
quiz.explain: Comparing two things, so we add -er: slower.
quiz.mistake: Uses -est for two things

teach.ask: Gappu is small, his sister is smaller and baby Pippi is the smallest. How do we compare two things and many things?
teach.praise: Excellent! Use -er and 'than' for two, and 'the' with -est for three or more. Pippi is the smallest, and the cutest!
teach.nudge: What do we add when comparing two? And when comparing three or more?

learn.hook: Stone steps, a river, an old fort and the clack-clack of looms. Welcome to Maheshwar!
points: The lesson 'Maheshwar' takes us to a town of rivers, forts and weaving.
Maheshwar is a town in Madhya Pradesh, on the banks of the river Narmada.
Ghats are wide steps that lead down to a river.
Rani Ahilyabai Holkar, a queen of the Holkar family, made Maheshwar her capital more than 250 years ago. The Ahilya Fort stands above the ghats.
The Narmada flows towards the west and falls into the Arabian Sea.

example.q: Read: Maheshwar is a small town in Madhya Pradesh, on the banks of the river Narmada. Long stone steps called ghats lead down to the water. Above the ghats stands the old Ahilya Fort. In many homes, you can hear the clack-clack of handlooms. Weavers make the famous Maheshwari sarees there, thread by thread. Question: Name two things you can see near the river in Maheshwar.
steps: Find the lines about the river.
'Long stone steps called ghats lead down to the water.'
'Above the ghats stands the old Ahilya Fort.'
example.answer: The ghats and the Ahilya Fort.

learn.reallife: Many Indian towns grew up on river banks, like Varanasi on the Ganga and Maheshwar on the Narmada.

learn.hook: Thread by thread, row by row, a beautiful saree grows on the loom!
points: A handloom is a loom worked by the weaver's hands and feet, without electricity.
The long threads on a loom are the warp. The threads that go across are the weft.
A shuttle carries the weft thread across the loom.
Maheshwari sarees are light sarees of cotton and silk. They are known for a border that can be worn on either side.
Heritage means the buildings, crafts, songs and ways of life from the past that we value and pass on. National Handloom Day is on 7 August.

Things from the past that we value and pass on are our heritage.
example.answer: Because it is an old craft that people value and pass on from one generation to the next.

learn.hook: maheshwar or Maheshwar? narmada or Narmada? Capital letters help special names stand tall!
points: Start every sentence with a capital letter.
Names of people, places, rivers, days and months begin with a capital letter: Ahilyabai, Maheshwar, Narmada, Monday, August.
The word 'I' is always a capital letter.
Names of seasons (winter, monsoon) do not need a capital letter unless they start a sentence.
Use commas to separate things in a list: We saw ghats, a fort and a loom. Also use a comma after 'Yes' or 'No' at the start: Yes, I can.

example.q: Think it through: correct this sentence: 'in august, meena saw cotton silk and gold thread in maheshwar.'
steps: Start the sentence with a capital: In.
Names of months, people and places need capitals: August, Meena, Maheshwar.
Put a comma between list items: cotton, silk and gold thread.
example.answer: In August, Meena saw cotton, silk and gold thread in Maheshwar.

learn.reallife: When you write your address on a letter or a parcel, the names of your street, city and state all need capital letters.

games.title: Capital letter or not?

games.title: Capitals and commas: true or false?
items: The word 'I' is always written as a capital letter.
Names of months begin with a capital letter.
We write January, August and so on.
We put commas between the things in a list.
Every word in a sentence starts with a capital letter.
Only the first word and special names need capitals.
The name of a river, like Narmada, starts with a small letter.
A river's name is a proper noun. It needs a capital letter.

quiz.q: In "We took a boat on the narmada.", which word needs a capital letter?
quiz.explain: Narmada is the name of a river, so it needs a capital N.
quiz.mistake: Thinks common words need capitals

quiz.q: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
options: We bought cotton, silk and thread.
We bought cotton silk and thread.
We bought, cotton, silk and thread.
We, bought cotton silk and thread.
quiz.explain: Commas go between the items of a list: cotton, silk and thread.
quiz.mistake: Puts commas in the wrong places or leaves them out

quiz.q: Which of these words should always begin with a capital letter?
quiz.explain: Days of the week are special names, so they always need a capital letter.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any noun needs a capital

quiz.q: Where should the comma go? "Yes I would like to visit Maheshwar."
quiz.explain: We put a comma after 'Yes' at the start: Yes, I would like to visit Maheshwar.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the comma rule for yes and no

quiz.q: Why does 'Ahilyabai' begin with a capital letter?
options: It is the name of a person
quiz.explain: Names of people are proper nouns and need a capital letter.
quiz.mistake: Thinks long words need capitals

quiz.q: Which list is written correctly?
quiz.explain: We put a comma between list items, and 'and' before the last one.
quiz.mistake: Leaves out commas or adds too many

quiz.q: Which word does NOT need a capital letter in the middle of a sentence?
quiz.explain: Seasons like winter are not special names, so they do not need a capital letter.
quiz.mistake: Thinks seasons are like months and days

quiz.q: Find the mistake: "My friend ravi lives in Indore."

quiz.mistake: Does not notice the small letter in the name
